title: Longest Word in Dictionary
prompt:
Given an array of strings `words` representing a dictionary, return the longest word in `words` that can be built one character at a time by other words in `words`. In other words, `word` qualifies only if every proper prefix of `word` (of length 1, 2, ..., len(word)-1) also appears in `words`.

If there is more than one qualifying word of the maximum length, return the lexicographically smallest one. If no word qualifies (not even a single character), return an empty string.

examples.explanation: "world" is buildable one letter at a time via "w" -> "wo" -> "wor" -> "worl" -> "world", all present in words.
Both "apple" and "apply" are buildable and have the same length 5; "apple" is lexicographically smaller.
"abc" requires "a" and "ab" to also be present in words to be buildable one letter at a time, but neither is, so no word qualifies and the result is an empty string.

constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters
hints: A word only qualifies if EVERY prefix of it (not just the immediate one) is also a full word in the list — checking that with a hash set repeatedly is possible but a trie makes the structure of 'buildable' explicit.
Insert all words into a trie, marking end-of-word nodes. A word is buildable exactly when every node along its path (excluding the root) is marked as an end-of-word node.
Do a DFS/BFS from the trie root that only continues into a child if that child is itself a word ending, tracking the longest (and lexicographically smallest on ties) word found along valid paths.

solution.approach: Insert every word into a trie, marking the end of each. Then traverse the trie starting from the root, but only allow descending into a child node if that child itself is marked as a word ending — that's exactly the condition that the prefix ending there is a real, previously-inserted word, enforcing the one-letter-at-a-time buildability requirement transitively. Track the best (longest, then lexicographically smallest) word seen during this restricted traversal. Sorting the input first and using a simple prefix-set check achieves the same result, but the trie traversal directly encodes the buildability chain.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(sum of word lengths) for the trie
